title: What does FATF Recommendation 16, the travel rule, require for virtual-asset transfers?
abstract: Sourced guide to how FATF Recommendation 16 applies to virtual-asset service providers: the information that travels with a transfer, the USD/EUR 1,000 option and its limits.
body:
According to FATF, Recommendation 16, the travel rule, applies to virtual-asset transfers: the originating provider must obtain required and accurate originator information and required beneficiary information and send it to the beneficiary institution immediately and securely. It must also make the information available to authorities. [1]

Countries may adopt a de minimis threshold of USD/EUR 1,000 for virtual-asset transfers, having regard to the risks. Below it the guidance still expects the names of the originator and the beneficiary and a wallet address or unique transaction reference; verifying that information is required where there is a suspicion of money laundering or terrorist financing. [1]

FATF separately sets the occasional-transaction threshold for customer due diligence by virtual asset service providers at USD/EUR 1,000, rather than the USD/EUR 15,000 that applies to other financial institutions. The rule attaches to regulated providers, and countries implement and supervise it through their own law, as FATF's 2025 paper on travel-rule supervision describes. [1][2]

Author interpretation: whether the rule binds a given business depends on whether national law treats it as a virtual asset service provider. Personal data does not belong in an on-ledger memo; it belongs in a private exchange between providers. A Testnet run shows a mechanism, not compliance. This summary rests on FATF's published guidance, not legal advice. Sources accessed 11 November 2026. [1][2]
